items.title: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992, section 188: Duty of employer to consult representatives
items.quote: shall be undertaken by the employer with a view to reaching agreement with the appropriate representatives
items.why: Where 20 or more redundancies are proposed at one establishment within 90 days, the employer must consult on ways of avoiding the dismissals, reducing their number and mitigating the consequences. The nearest UK law comes to requiring that elimination be tested against alternatives. Amended by the Employment Rights Act 2025 s.29, shown as in force for specified purposes only.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 172: Duty to promote the success of the company
items.quote: the interests of the company's employees
items.why: Directors must have regard to employees' interests and to long-term consequences when deciding how to promote the company's success. A duty to consider, not a duty to keep jobs.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in UK businesses: 2023 to 2026
items.quote: Most businesses report that the use of AI has not resulted in a change to their overall workforce headcount so far
items.why: Source of the figure: among medium-sized businesses, 'just under 7% reporting a decrease' in headcount. Self-reported, from the Business Insights and Conditions Survey (Wave 159: 26.7% response rate, 38,637 businesses). Measures headcount, not job redesign.

items.title: Assessment of AI capabilities and the impact on the UK labour market
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and AI Security Institute
items.locator: Figure 2 and the paragraph above it
items.quote: Around half of exposed workers are in ‘high complementarity’ roles.
items.why: The government's own reading of where AI is more likely to support than replace work: UK 35% high exposure and high complementarity, 32% high exposure and low complementarity, using an IMF measure. The report calls the indices indicative, not precise.

items.title: Generative AI at Work
items.publisher: Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li and Lindsey Raymond (arXiv preprint 2304.11771)
items.quote: Access to AI assistance increases worker productivity, as measured by issues resolved per hour, by 15% on average
items.why: The main field study of AI used to assist, not replace: 5,172 customer-support agents, with the largest gains for less experienced workers. Authors' preprint, version dated 7 November 2024; the earlier NBER working paper (w31161) reported 14%. One firm, one occupation.

items.title: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.publisher: Shakked Noy and Whitney Zhang, MIT (working paper)
items.quote: ChatGPT mostly substitutes for worker effort rather than complementing worker skills
items.why: The counterweight: in an experiment with 444 professionals, output improved but the tool mostly replaced effort. Augmentation is a design choice, not an automatic result. Authors' working paper, marked not peer reviewed; the published version in Science refused access and was not read.

items.title: The Turing Trap: The Promise & Peril of Human-Like Artificial Intelligence
items.publisher: Erik Brynjolfsson, Stanford Digital Economy Lab (arXiv preprint 2201.04200)
items.quote: when AI is focused on augmenting humans rather than mimicking them, then humans retain the power to insist on a share of the value created
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation. The argument for augmentation as an ethical and economic choice: substitution moves bargaining power from workers to whoever controls the technology. An essay, not an empirical study. Author's preprint; the Daedalus version refused access.

items.title: Generative AI and Jobs: A global analysis of potential effects on job quantity and quality (ILO Working Paper 96)
items.quote: In low-income countries, only 0.4 per cent of total employment is potentially exposed to automation effects
items.why: International comparator. Separates automation potential from augmentation potential by occupation and finds the larger effect is augmentation; 5.5% of employment in high-income countries is exposed to automation. An upper-bound estimate of exposure, not a forecast.

items.title: The Future of Jobs Report 2025
items.locator: Key findings, page 6; chapter 2, 'The shifting human-machine frontier: automation versus augmentation'
items.quote: 40% anticipate reducing their workforce where AI can automate tasks
items.why: What employers say they intend: an employer survey, so a statement of plans, not outcomes. The same report says technology can be designed to complement human work and that this depends on choices made now.

items.title: The Wrong Kind of AI? Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Labor Demand (IZA Discussion Paper No. 12292)
items.publisher: Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo, IZA Institute of Labor Economics
items.quote: Recent technological change has been biased towards automation, with insufficient focus on creating new tasks where labor can be productively employed.
items.why: The economic argument behind an augmentation-first default: AI can either automate existing tasks or create new ones in which people are productive, and the authors argue the balance has tilted too far to automation, with stagnating labour demand and lower productivity growth as the result. Limits: a discussion paper (the series says papers 'often represent preliminary work'); an argument paper written in 2019, before generative AI; not a study of firms' strategies.

items.title: New Frontiers: The Origins and Content of New Work, 1940-2018 (NBER Working Paper 30389)
items.publisher: David Autor, Caroline Chin, Anna Salomons and Bryan Seegmiller, National Bureau of Economic Research
items.quote: the demand-eroding effects of automation innovations have intensified in the last four decades while the demand-increasing effects of augmentation innovations have not
items.why: The strongest empirical base found for the distinction the criterion rests on: over eight decades of United States data, innovations that augment an occupation's output raise demand for its labour and generate new kinds of work, while innovations that automate its tasks depress demand. Limits: United States census and patent data; the working paper states it has not been peer reviewed (a later journal version was not read); occupation-level, so it does not show that an individual firm choosing augmentation does better.

items.title: Can we Have Pro-Worker AI? Choosing a path of machines in service of minds (policy memo)
items.publisher: Daron Acemoglu, David Autor and Simon Johnson, MIT Shaping the Future of Work Initiative
items.quote: Choosing the human-complementary path is feasible but will require changes in the direction of technological innovation, as well as in corporate norms and behavior.
items.why: States the criterion's premise directly for generative AI: the path is a choice, and making AI complement workers needs changes in corporate norms as well as in technology. Useful for a board because it describes what 'human-complementary' use looks like in practice (tools that let more people do expert work). Limits: a policy memo by three economists, not peer reviewed; its recommendations are for United States federal policy; argument, not new evidence. The summary's text layer has irregular spacing in places.

items.title: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects (Becker Friedman Institute Working Paper No. 2025-56)
items.publisher: Anders Humlum and Emilie Vestergaard, University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute
items.locator: Abstract (PDF page 2); Introduction for the share of workers with new tasks
items.quote: AI chatbots have had no significant impact on earnings or recorded hours in any occupation
items.why: The best measured evidence found on what AI chatbots have done to jobs so far: two surveys of 25,000 workers in 7,000 Danish workplaces linked to administrative records show no effect on earnings or hours, average time savings of 2.8%, and new job tasks created for 8.4% of workers. It supports measuring redesign and new tasks, and cautions against business cases built on headcount savings. Limits: Denmark; 11 exposed occupations; surveys in late 2023 and 2024; working paper, not peer reviewed.

items.title: Transformed by AI: How generative artificial intelligence could affect work in the UK - and how to manage it
items.publisher: Carsten Jung and Bhargav Srinivasa Desikan, Institute for Public Policy Research
items.quote: In our 'full augmentation' scenario we show that there can be zero job displacement.
items.why: A UK analysis that sets augmentation and displacement side by side: assessing 22,000 tasks, it models a full augmentation scenario (no jobs lost, 13 per cent added to GDP), a full displacement scenario (8 million jobs lost, no GDP gain) and a central case between them. It gives a board UK numbers for why the default matters. Limits: think-tank scenario modelling, which the authors say are 'not predictions'; not peer reviewed; economy-wide, not firm-level; published March 2024.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 414CB: Contents of non-financial and sustainability information statement
items.quote: a description of the outcome of those policies
items.why: The binding UK reporting rule nearest to 'measured and reported': companies within section 414CA must report on the company's employees in the strategic report, including the policies pursued, the outcome of those policies, the principal risks and the non-financial key performance indicators. An augmentation-first policy and its results would sit here. Limits: applies only to the kinds of company described in section 414CA(1), which was not read in this pass; it does not mention AI, automation or job design; a company may explain that it has no policy.

items.title: OECD AI Principles, Principle 2.4: Building human capacity and preparing for labour market transformation
items.publisher: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD.AI)
items.locator: Rationale for this principle, third paragraph
items.quote: to be able to leverage AI in their areas of expertise, so that AI augments human capabilities
items.why: International comparator. The OECD's intergovernmental AI standard treats augmentation as the aim: skills policy should let workers use AI in their own fields 'so that AI augments human capabilities', and governments should promote responsible use of AI at work to improve job quality. Limits: a recommendation addressed to governments, not a duty on firms; non-binding; the page carries no date (the OECD's principles page says they were adopted in 2019 and updated in May 2024).

items.title: Managing technology that manages people: November 2025. A Social Partnership approach to algorithmic management systems in the Welsh public sector
items.publisher: Welsh Government (guidance agreed by the Workforce Partnership Council)
items.quote: A commitment to protecting jobs, creating jobs, and investing in the workforce.
items.why: A UK example of a stated augmentation-first position: the Welsh Government, devolved public sector employers and trade unions have agreed, as a general principle for any algorithmic management system, a commitment to protect and create jobs and invest in the workforce. It is what a 'stated policy' at the Defined level can look like. Limits: devolved public sector in Wales only; guidance, not law; covers systems used to manage workers, not all AI; it sets no metrics.
